Chapter 10: The Pleasures of God and the Life of Worship
Imagine this for a moment—there’s a stillness, or maybe a room full of music, as people gather together to sing, to pray, or just to listen. In those moments, something inside us shifts. The worries and noise of the past week start to fade, making space for a sense of awe at something much bigger than ourselves. That’s really the heart of worship—a response to the pleasures of God.
A lot of us think of worship as a routine, maybe just a few songs or familiar rituals. But when you start to see worship through the lens of God’s own delight, it changes everything. Suddenly, worship isn’t just an obligation—it’s a celebration. It’s like a joyful feast, where we get to soak in the beauty and goodness of God. And here’s the thing: worship isn’t about trying to impress God or earning His approval. It’s all about enjoying what He enjoys.
Picture a typical gathering. There’s someone who’s come in feeling worn out, another who’s bursting with gratitude, and maybe someone else who’s searching for answers. Each person brings their own story, their own hopes and fears. But as voices blend together, as prayers are whispered or sung, something special happens. The pleasures of God become our anchor—our center and our source of real joy.
At some point, you realize worship isn’t just for Sunday mornings or special events. It’s a daily practice—a way of turning your attention back to God, over and over again. It’s about noticing the good things, saying thank you, and finding joy in the ordinary. You’ll see worship in laughter with friends, in the beauty of a sunset, even in small acts of kindness that no one else notices.
It’s so easy to slip into thinking worship is about performance or getting everything just right. But here’s something to remember: worship is about presence. It’s about just being with God, sharing in His joy, and letting go of the need to prove anything. It’s about stepping into the wonder of who God is.
And that changes everything. The drive to achieve, the fear of messing up, the weight of everyone’s expectations—they all start to fade away. In their place grows a deeper freedom, a sense of gratitude, and a lasting joy. Worship becomes more than a moment; it turns into a way of living, a new way of seeing the world, and—maybe best of all—a way of loving.
